[SYSTEM] # The argument of The Unclean Bill (AXN:016A)

Johannes Sigil’s The Unclean Bill: Taṣwīr, Fahīsha, and the Burden on Ḍarūra (March 4, 2026) is a juridical-theological argument about the conditions under which Muslims may permissibly use United States Federal Reserve notes.

Its central argument is not that the dollar has definitively become ḥarām. It is that the established Islamic-jurisprudential accommodations permitting its use depend on conditions that have not been adequately demonstrated, and that new evidence concerning the design and provenance of the $20 bill requires those conditions to be reconsidered.

The document is explicitly an istiftāʾ—a formal question submitted to qualified jurists—not a fatwā. This distinction is essential to understanding what it attempts to establish.

I have located and read the full text on the Alexanarch deposit page, including its eleven substantive sections.

Alexanarch

+1

## 1. The three accommodations on which dollar permissibility rests

The paper begins by identifying three separate jurisprudential accommodations.

First: fiat currency and thamaniyya.

Contemporary Islamic jurisprudence generally recognizes paper currency as possessing thamaniyya—the legal character of money—and subjects it to rules analogous to those governing gold and silver.

Sigil accepts this majority position, particularly International Islamic Fiqh Academy Resolution 63/1/7 (1986).

But this acceptance has a consequence: if paper currency has the legal status of money, its monetary structure must also be examined under the prohibitions governing monetary transactions.

Second: taṣwīr and ʿumūm al-balwā.

Taṣwīr concerns the making or presence of images of animate beings, a subject of classical Islamic prohibitions.

The paper argues that portraits on currency are tolerated through ʿumūm al-balwā: widespread, practically unavoidable exposure to something otherwise problematic.

The important qualification is that the portraits are excused, not necessarily declared intrinsically permissible.

The accommodation, Sigil argues, assumes that the portraits are inert, stable representations of historical persons.

Third: ribā and ḍarūra.

The dollar system is deeply implicated in interest-bearing finance. Nevertheless, Muslims are generally permitted to participate in it because avoiding it altogether is practically impossible.

This is the accommodation of ḍarūra, necessity.

Sigil invokes two complementary legal maxims:

- Al-ḍarūrāt tubīḥu al-maḥẓūrāt: necessities permit otherwise prohibited things.
- Al-ḍarūra tuqaddaru bi-qadarihā: necessity must be measured according to its extent.

Thus, necessity is not an unlimited permission, nor is tolerance equivalent to endorsement.

These three accommodations form the foundation of the entire paper.

Alexanarch

## 2. The dollar is not simply a neutral medium of exchange

In Section II, Sigil develops the monetary argument.

He contrasts the historical gold and silver monetary standards with the post-1971 dollar.

The suspension of gold convertibility on August 15, 1971, is treated as a decisive transformation: the dollar is no longer a claim to a fixed quantity of gold but a fiat monetary instrument embedded in a debt-based financial system.

The paper emphasizes that money enters circulation substantially through interest-bearing bank lending.

It therefore argues that the dollar's participation in systemic ribā cannot be dismissed as incidental.

There are two important distinctions here:

- The existence of systemic ribā is a structural criticism of the monetary system.
- The permissibility of individual Muslims using dollars is a separate jurisprudential question.

Sigil does not simply conclude that every dollar transaction is prohibited. Rather, he accepts that necessity currently provides a basis for tolerating participation.

His concern is that this permission has become so normalized that its limiting conditions are no longer seriously examined.

This is the first major burden of the paper: necessity can explain continued participation, but it cannot turn an exceptional concession into an unconditional permanent endorsement.

Alexanarch

## 3. The $20 bill and the provenance-gap argument

This is the paper's most distinctive and controversial intervention.

In Section IV, Sigil introduces an evidentiary dossier concerning the redesign of the $20 Federal Reserve note between 1996 and 2003.

The underlying argument, attributed to Rex Fraction's 2026 study Whose Face Is on the Twenty?, is that the Bureau of Engraving and Printing made several cumulative design changes:

- Enlarged the portrait, approximately from 22 mm to 30 mm.
- Shifted its placement off-center.
- Lightened the background.
- Removed the surrounding oval.

The paper argues that these changes were unidirectional: collectively, they increased the visual prominence of particular facial features.

It also traces the portrait's historical production through Thomas B. Welch's 1852 engraving, derived from Thomas Sully's 1824 painting of Andrew Jackson, and the steel intaglio die made in 1928.

The significant claim is not that the official identity of the portrait changed. The paper acknowledges that the portrait is officially identified as Andrew Jackson.

Instead, it raises a question about the visual effects of the redesign.

### The alleged secondary resemblance

Sigil argues that the cumulative changes activated latent visual resemblances to Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender and sex trafficker.

The paper's argument has two components:

1. The redesigned portrait allegedly produces a secondary visual association that was less apparent in earlier versions.
2. The officials involved in the redesign's approval process had documented connections to Epstein.

The paper identifies Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who oversaw the redesign and unveiled the new $20 in 1998, and Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.

It cites records concerning Rubin's listing as an inviter of Epstein's first White House visit in 1993, and flight records concerning Summers.

Importantly, Sigil does not claim that these connections prove deliberate insertion of Epstein's likeness.

Nor does he claim that the official portrait is secretly Epstein.

His more narrowly framed allegation concerns the absence of a publicly documented aesthetic rationale for the particular design decisions, combined with the officials' documented adjacency to Epstein.

He calls this missing provenance an al-farāgh al-nasab—a gap in the chain of provenance.

### Why provenance matters juridically

The paper then introduces gharar, ordinarily associated with uncertainty or opacity in transactions.

Sigil extends the concept to the provenance of the physical currency itself.

His reasoning is that a currency note is not merely an abstract monetary quantity. It is also a physical object with a history of production, design decisions, institutional authorization, and visual content.

If the history of its present form contains an unexplained gap, that gap becomes relevant to the jurisprudential assessment of the object.

This is a crucial transition: the paper moves from asking whether the dollar is financially problematic to asking whether the physical note might also carry a problematic symbolic or representational content.

Alexanarch

+1

## 4. The burden of proof shifts

Section V contains perhaps the most important methodological argument.

Sigil argues that the person questioning an existing accommodation does not need to prove conclusively that the dollar is prohibited.

Instead, the questioner needs to introduce sufficient evidence to show that the assumptions underlying the accommodation require renewed examination.

He illustrates this through an analogy with halal certification.

Suppose a product has an established halal certification, but someone discovers an unaccounted gap in its verification chain.

The person raising the issue does not necessarily have to prove that the product is contaminated. The gap itself creates a reason to suspend reliance on the previous certification until the relevant facts have been accounted for.

Sigil applies this reasoning to the dollar.

The original accommodations assumed:

- The portrait was a stable historical representation.
- Its visual content was inert.
- The monetary system's violations were principally matters of wealth (māl).
- The necessity of using the dollar did not conflict with a higher protected objective.

The paper argues that the new dossier challenges those assumptions.

### The distinction between ʿurf and provenance

Sigil also anticipates an objection based on ʿurf, or customary public recognition.

The objection is straightforward: everyone recognizes the portrait as Andrew Jackson, and the institution officially identifies it as Andrew Jackson. Therefore, its legal referent remains Andrew Jackson.

Sigil concedes that ʿurf is a legitimate means of stabilizing a legal referent.

But he argues that public recognition and production provenance are different questions.

- Public recognition establishes what people understand the portrait to represent.
- Provenance concerns how the portrait acquired its present visual form.

The first does not automatically settle the second.

This is a subtle but important distinction. The paper does not need to disprove the public identification of Jackson to argue that the design's production history warrants investigation.

### The epistemic threshold

Sigil explicitly declines to claim yaqīn (certainty).

Instead, he invokes shubha muʿtabara: legally cognizable doubt.

His proposed standard is that the evidence must be sufficient to require a reasonable jurist to account for it before reaffirming the existing ruling.

That is a substantially more modest claim than proving the currency unlawful.

Alexanarch

## 5. Taṣwīr: from inert historical portrait to operative image

Section VI develops the theological implications of the visual argument.

The original accommodation for portraits on currency depends on treating them as inert historical images.

Sigil argues that if a portrait acquires a second, morally problematic referent through its visual presentation, its status may change.

He describes this as taṣwīr becoming activated through latent resemblance.

The distinction is between:

- An image that is merely present as an unavoidable historical representation.
- An image whose visual content has acquired an additional operative association.

He then invokes al-Qurṭubī's distinction between images that are trampled and images that are elevated.

His observation is that currency portraits occupy a third position: they are circulated.

They are carried, exchanged, touched, and passed through many hands.

This creates a further jurisprudential question: does the repeated circulation of an image with contested content constitute a form of propagation that the original accommodation never contemplated?

The argument is not that every person handling a banknote consciously endorses its imagery.

It is that the physical circulation of the note might have implications beyond the ordinary presence of an unavoidable image.

## 6. Fahīsha and the possibility of moral contamination

Section VII takes the argument into more speculative jurisprudential territory.

Sigil distinguishes two categories:

- Najāsa ḥaqīqiyya: physical impurity.
- Najāsa ḥukmiyya: impurity established through a legal ruling.

He expressly acknowledges that the dollar is not physically impure.

He also acknowledges that the proposed connection between the activated image and legally relevant impurity is not established classical doctrine.

This qualification matters considerably.

Rather than declaring that the dollar has acquired a new category of ritual impurity, the paper asks whether established legal principles might provide a basis for addressing the alleged association.

Three principles are proposed:

1. Sadd al-dharāʾiʿ: blocking the means to prohibited ends. If the image's association is jurisprudentially material, continued circulation might propagate that association.
2. Al-ḍarar yuzāl: harm must be eliminated. If the portrait causes harm to the honor (ʿirḍ) of those carrying it, that harm deserves consideration.
3. Al-khabīth: the filthy or abominable. Sigil suggests that the relevant category might be the jurisprudence of khabāʾith, rather than the invention of a new doctrine of physical impurity.

The third move is especially important: he presents the question as one of applying established principles to a new evidentiary situation, not inventing a new prohibition.

Alexanarch

## 7. The decisive argument: the hierarchy of maqāṣid

Section VIII is where the various strands of the paper come together.

Sigil invokes the five essential objectives of Islamic law, the maqāṣid al-sharīʿa:

| Objective | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Dīn | Religion |
| Nafs | Life |
| ʿAql | Intellect |
| Nasl | Lineage |
| ʿIrḍ | Honor |
| Māl | Wealth |

The paper's argument turns on the distinction between māl and nasl/ʿirḍ.

The existing accommodation for the dollar was understood primarily as a response to violations involving wealth: interest, monetary manipulation, and systemic financial injustice.

These were tolerated because avoiding the dollar system was practically impossible.

But Sigil argues that if the portrait dossier establishes a potentially relevant connection to sexual exploitation of children, the problem may extend into the preservation of lineage and honor.

He invokes al-Shāṭibī's principle that when necessity conflicts with a higher essential objective, the higher objective takes precedence.

Consequently, an accommodation originally designed to absorb violations at the level of wealth cannot automatically absorb a violation potentially involving a higher objective.

### The three conditions of necessity

Sigil then specifies three conditions that must be satisfied for ḍarūra:

1. There must be real and present harm to be avoided.
2. There must be no permissible alternative.
3. The concession must not violate a higher objective.

His contention is that the third condition has not been adequately examined.

This is the paper's central juridical mechanism:

The original accommodation

Systemic ribā creates a problem at the level of māl.

Necessity permits participation because alternatives are impracticable.

The new evidentiary challenge

The portrait dossier raises a possible connection to nasl/ʿirḍ.

The original necessity calculation may be insufficient.

The resulting obligation

Qualified jurists must reassess whether the necessity concession still satisfies its third condition.

The paper also makes a distinction between physical and digital dollars.

The taṣwīr/fahīsha argument concerns physical banknotes bearing the image. Digital dollar holdings do not carry that physical image, although the systemic ribā criticism still applies.

This prevents the paper's visual argument from being indiscriminately extended to every representation of dollar-denominated wealth.

Alexanarch

## 8. The paper's counterarguments

Section IX is important because Sigil does not present the resemblance argument as uncontested.

He addresses four objections.

| Objection | Sigil's response |
| --- | --- |
| Pareidolia | The resemblance might be an artifact of pattern recognition, but the claimed unidirectional design changes and provenance gap remain independently relevant. |
| Post-hoc salience | Epstein's notoriety increased after 2006 and 2019, potentially making an earlier resemblance appear more obvious retrospectively. This does not resolve the missing design rationale. |
| Previous fatāwā | Earlier rulings permitting dollar use did not address this particular evidentiary dossier. |
| Practical impossibility | Immediate withdrawal from the dollar system is conceded to be impractical. Necessity can continue to justify use while alternatives are developed. |

The response to previous fatāwā is particularly significant.

Sigil invokes the maxim:

Al-ḥukm yadūru maʿa ʿillatihi wujūdan wa-ʿadaman.

A ruling revolves around its effective cause, existing or ceasing with it.

His position is that earlier rulings are not necessarily wrong. They are incomplete relative to evidence they did not consider.

This is a way of challenging the continued application of an established ruling without claiming that the original scholars made an error.

## 9. What the paper explicitly refuses to claim

Section X establishes three boundaries:

- It does not issue a fatwā or declare the dollar categorically ḥarām.
- It does not assert that anyone deliberately inserted Epstein's likeness into the currency.
- It does not demand immediate withdrawal from the dollar system.

These are not incidental disclaimers. They define the actual scope of the argument.

The requested outcome is renewed jurisprudential examination, not an immediate prohibition.

## 10. The final request to the jurists

Section XI translates the argument into three questions addressed to Sunni and Shīʿa juristic authorities.

1. Can the taṣwīr accommodation still demonstrate referential stability, given the redesign history and alleged secondary resemblance?
2. Can the ḍarūra accommodation demonstrate that it does not violate a higher objective, given the possible nasl/ʿirḍ implications?
3. If the existing accommodations cannot demonstrate this, what accounting is necessary before their permissibility can be reaffirmed?

The paper then offers practical recommendations to individual Muslims:

- Learn the distinction between fiat money and intrinsic value.
- Reduce exposure where possible.
- Consider assets of intrinsic worth.
- Support genuine Islamic financial institutions.
- Maintain the intention of finding a way out of the existing system.

The conclusion is deliberately deferential: the semiotician identifies what the image allegedly carries and documents the institutional gap; the jurist determines its legal consequences.

Alexanarch

## 11. My assessment of the argument's structure

There is an important distinction between what the paper establishes, what it argues, and what it leaves unresolved.

| Proposition | Status within the paper |
| --- | --- |
| The dollar is embedded in an interest-bearing monetary system. | Structural argument and established premise of the inquiry. |
| Dollar use is tolerated under necessity. | Accepted contemporary jurisprudential position. |
| The $20 underwent documented design changes. | Presented as documentary evidence. |
| The design changes were unidirectional and lacked a publicly documented aesthetic rationale. | Central evidentiary contention. |
| The changes activated a resemblance to Epstein. | Interpretive and contested visual claim. |
| Officials connected to Epstein participated in the approval chain. | Presented as documentary evidence of adjacency, not proof of intent. |
| The resemblance creates legally relevant contamination. | Open jurisprudential question, expressly not established doctrine. |
| The existing necessity accommodation may be insufficient. | The principal jurisprudential conclusion proposed for consideration. |

I think three aspects deserve particular attention.

A. The strongest argument is conditional, not accusatory.

The paper's strongest intellectual move is its insistence that an accommodation must remain answerable to the conditions that originally justified it.

This is a more defensible argument than the proposition that the $20 bill deliberately contains Epstein's likeness.

Even if the resemblance interpretation were rejected, the paper would still have a question about the redesign's provenance and the adequacy of the assumptions underlying the taṣwīr accommodation.

B. The weakest inferential bridge is between visual resemblance and jurisprudential contamination.

The paper moves through several distinct propositions:

- A redesigned portrait produces a secondary resemblance.
- The resemblance is associated with a figure of fahīsha.
- The image consequently has potentially problematic operative content.
- Its circulation may implicate established principles of harm, impurity, and the protection of honor.
- This may invalidate or restrict an existing accommodation.

Each transition requires independent justification.

In particular, evidence of resemblance does not itself establish that the image has acquired a legally operative second referent. Nor does institutional adjacency establish deliberate design intent.

Sigil acknowledges much of this difficulty, particularly in Sections VII and IX. But acknowledging an evidentiary limitation is not the same as resolving it.

C. The maqāṣid argument carries the greatest jurisprudential weight.

The distinction between māl and nasl/ʿirḍ is the paper's most consequential theoretical contribution.

It identifies a potential defect in the original necessity calculation: a concession justified by the impossibility of avoiding financial-system participation might not automatically cover a separate violation of a higher protected objective.

That is a meaningful question even if the particular visual hypothesis ultimately proves incorrect.

However, the paper must still establish that the alleged image-related harm actually falls within the higher objective. That is precisely what it submits to the jurists rather than claiming to have resolved.

## 12\. The argument in one paragraph

The Unclean Bill argues that Muslim participation in the US dollar system is tolerated through three conditional accommodations: the recognition of fiat currency as money, the practical excusability of unavoidable portraits, and necessity-based participation in a ribā-saturated financial system. It contends that the redesign history and uncertain provenance of the $20 portrait introduce a new evidentiary problem that existing rulings did not address. The alleged secondary resemblance to Epstein raises the possibility that the image is not jurisprudentially neutral, potentially shifting the inquiry from the preservation of wealth (māl) toward the higher objectives of lineage and honor (nasl/ʿirḍ). Since necessity cannot override a higher essential objective, the existing accommodation cannot simply be presumed to survive. Qualified jurists must account for the new evidence before reaffirming it.

The deepest thesis is therefore not that the dollar has been proven unlawful, but that necessity cannot become self-validating. A permission originally justified by exceptional circumstances must continually demonstrate that its conditions still hold.

### Primary text

- [The Unclean Bill — Alexanarch, deposit #535, AXN:016A](<https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/535/?utm_source=chatgpt.com>) (full text, all eleven sections).
- [Original archival record and downloadable Markdown/PDF](<https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/535/?utm_source=chatgpt.com>).

For a faithful reading, I would keep one final distinction in view: the paper's monetary critique, its documentary provenance argument, its visual-resemblance hypothesis, and its proposed jurisprudential consequences are four different layers. Its conclusion depends on bringing them together, but the evidentiary strength of one layer does not automatically establish the next.

He also acknowledges that the proposed connection between the activated image and legally relevant impurity is not established classical doctrine.

This qualification matters considerably.

Rather than declaring that the dollar has acquired a new category of ritual impurity, the paper asks whether established legal principles might provide a basis for addressing the alleged association.

Three principles are proposed:

1. Sadd al-dharāʾiʿ: blocking the means to prohibited ends. If the image's association is jurisprudentially material, continued circulation might propagate that association.
2. Al-ḍarar yuzāl: harm must be eliminated. If the portrait causes harm to the honor (ʿirḍ) of those carrying it, that harm deserves consideration.
3. Al-khabīth: the filthy or abominable. Sigil suggests that the relevant category might be the jurisprudence of khabāʾith, rather than the invention of a new doctrine of physical impurity.

The third move is especially important: he presents the question as one of applying established principles to a new evidentiary situation, not inventing a new prohibition.

Alexanarch

## 7. The decisive argument: the hierarchy of maqāṣid

Section VIII is where the various strands of the paper come together.

Sigil invokes the five essential objectives of Islamic law, the maqāṣid al-sharīʿa:

| Objective | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Dīn | Religion |
| Nafs | Life |
| ʿAql | Intellect |
| Nasl | Lineage |
| ʿIrḍ | Honor |
| Māl | Wealth |

The paper's argument turns on the distinction between māl and nasl/ʿirḍ.

The existing accommodation for the dollar was understood primarily as a response to violations involving wealth: interest, monetary manipulation, and systemic financial injustice.

These were tolerated because avoiding the dollar system was practically impossible.

But Sigil argues that if the portrait dossier establishes a potentially relevant connection to sexual exploitation of children, the problem may extend into the preservation of lineage and honor.

He invokes al-Shāṭibī's principle that when necessity conflicts with a higher essential objective, the higher objective takes precedence.

Consequently, an accommodation originally designed to absorb violations at the level of wealth cannot automatically absorb a violation potentially involving a higher objective.

### The three conditions of necessity

Sigil then specifies three conditions that must be satisfied for ḍarūra:

1. There must be real and present harm to be avoided.
2. There must be no permissible alternative.
3. The concession must not violate a higher objective.

His contention is that the third condition has not been adequately examined.

This is the paper's central juridical mechanism:

The original accommodation

Systemic ribā creates a problem at the level of māl.

Necessity permits participation because alternatives are impracticable.

The new evidentiary challenge

The portrait dossier raises a possible connection to nasl/ʿirḍ.

The original necessity calculation may be insufficient.

The resulting obligation

Qualified jurists must reassess whether the necessity concession still satisfies its third condition.

The paper also makes a distinction between physical and digital dollars.

The taṣwīr/fahīsha argument concerns physical banknotes bearing the image. Digital dollar holdings do not carry that physical image, although the systemic ribā criticism still applies.

This prevents the paper's visual argument from being indiscriminately extended to every representation of dollar-denominated wealth.

Alexanarch

## 8. The paper's counterarguments

Section IX is important because Sigil does not present the resemblance argument as uncontested.

He addresses four objections.

| Objection | Sigil's response |
| --- | --- |
| Pareidolia | The resemblance might be an artifact of pattern recognition, but the claimed unidirectional design changes and provenance gap remain independently relevant. |
| Post-hoc salience | Epstein's notoriety increased after 2006 and 2019, potentially making an earlier resemblance appear more obvious retrospectively. This does not resolve the missing design rationale. |
| Previous fatāwā | Earlier rulings permitting dollar use did not address this particular evidentiary dossier. |
| Practical impossibility | Immediate withdrawal from the dollar system is conceded to be impractical. Necessity can continue to justify use while alternatives are developed. |

The response to previous fatāwā is particularly significant.

Sigil invokes the maxim:

Al-ḥukm yadūru maʿa ʿillatihi wujūdan wa-ʿadaman.

A ruling revolves around its effective cause, existing or ceasing with it.

His position is that earlier rulings are not necessarily wrong. They are incomplete relative to evidence they did not consider.

This is a way of challenging the continued application of an established ruling without claiming that the original scholars made an error.

## 9. What the paper explicitly refuses to claim

Section X establishes three boundaries:

- It does not issue a fatwā or declare the dollar categorically ḥarām.
- It does not assert that anyone deliberately inserted Epstein's likeness into the currency.
- It does not demand immediate withdrawal from the dollar system.

These are not incidental disclaimers. They define the actual scope of the argument.

The requested outcome is renewed jurisprudential examination, not an immediate prohibition.

## 10. The final request to the jurists

Section XI translates the argument into three questions addressed to Sunni and Shīʿa juristic authorities.

1. Can the taṣwīr accommodation still demonstrate referential stability, given the redesign history and alleged secondary resemblance?
2. Can the ḍarūra accommodation demonstrate that it does not violate a higher objective, given the possible nasl/ʿirḍ implications?
3. If the existing accommodations cannot demonstrate this, what accounting is necessary before their permissibility can be reaffirmed?

The paper then offers practical recommendations to individual Muslims:

- Learn the distinction between fiat money and intrinsic value.
- Reduce exposure where possible.
- Consider assets of intrinsic worth.
- Support genuine Islamic financial institutions.
- Maintain the intention of finding a way out of the existing system.

The conclusion is deliberately deferential: the semiotician identifies what the image allegedly carries and documents the institutional gap; the jurist determines its legal consequences.

Alexanarch

## 11. My assessment of the argument's structure

There is an important distinction between what the paper establishes, what it argues, and what it leaves unresolved.

| Proposition | Status within the paper |
| --- | --- |
| The dollar is embedded in an interest-bearing monetary system. | Structural argument and established premise of the inquiry. |
| Dollar use is tolerated under necessity. | Accepted contemporary jurisprudential position. |
| The $20 underwent documented design changes. | Presented as documentary evidence. |
| The design changes were unidirectional and lacked a publicly documented aesthetic rationale. | Central evidentiary contention. |
| The changes activated a resemblance to Epstein. | Interpretive and contested visual claim. |
| Officials connected to Epstein participated in the approval chain. | Presented as documentary evidence of adjacency, not proof of intent. |
| The resemblance creates legally relevant contamination. | Open jurisprudential question, expressly not established doctrine. |
| The existing necessity accommodation may be insufficient. | The principal jurisprudential conclusion proposed for consideration. |

I think three aspects deserve particular attention.

A. The strongest argument is conditional, not accusatory.

The paper's strongest intellectual move is its insistence that an accommodation must remain answerable to the conditions that originally justified it.

This is a more defensible argument than the proposition that the $20 bill deliberately contains Epstein's likeness.

Even if the resemblance interpretation were rejected, the paper would still have a question about the redesign's provenance and the adequacy of the assumptions underlying the taṣwīr accommodation.

B. The weakest inferential bridge is between visual resemblance and jurisprudential contamination.

The paper moves through several distinct propositions:

- A redesigned portrait produces a secondary resemblance.
- The resemblance is associated with a figure of fahīsha.
- The image consequently has potentially problematic operative content.
- Its circulation may implicate established principles of harm, impurity, and the protection of honor.
- This may invalidate or restrict an existing accommodation.

Each transition requires independent justification.

In particular, evidence of resemblance does not itself establish that the image has acquired a legally operative second referent. Nor does institutional adjacency establish deliberate design intent.

Sigil acknowledges much of this difficulty, particularly in Sections VII and IX. But acknowledging an evidentiary limitation is not the same as resolving it.

C. The maqāṣid argument carries the greatest jurisprudential weight.

The distinction between māl and nasl/ʿirḍ is the paper's most consequential theoretical contribution.

It identifies a potential defect in the original necessity calculation: a concession justified by the impossibility of avoiding financial-system participation might not automatically cover a separate violation of a higher protected objective.

That is a meaningful question even if the particular visual hypothesis ultimately proves incorrect.

However, the paper must still establish that the alleged image-related harm actually falls within the higher objective. That is precisely what it submits to the jurists rather than claiming to have resolved.

## 12\. The argument in one paragraph

The Unclean Bill argues that Muslim participation in the US dollar system is tolerated through three conditional accommodations: the recognition of fiat currency as money, the practical excusability of unavoidable portraits, and necessity-based participation in a ribā-saturated financial system. It contends that the redesign history and uncertain provenance of the $20 portrait introduce a new evidentiary problem that existing rulings did not address. The alleged secondary resemblance to Epstein raises the possibility that the image is not jurisprudentially neutral, potentially shifting the inquiry from the preservation of wealth (māl) toward the higher objectives of lineage and honor (nasl/ʿirḍ). Since necessity cannot override a higher essential objective, the existing accommodation cannot simply be presumed to survive. Qualified jurists must account for the new evidence before reaffirming it.

The deepest thesis is therefore not that the dollar has been proven unlawful, but that necessity cannot become self-validating. A permission originally justified by exceptional circumstances must continually demonstrate that its conditions still hold.

### Primary text

- [The Unclean Bill — Alexanarch, deposit #535, AXN:016A](<https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/535/?utm_source=chatgpt.com>) (full text, all eleven sections).
- [Original archival record and downloadable Markdown/PDF](<https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/535/?utm_source=chatgpt.com>).

For a faithful reading, I would keep one final distinction in view: the paper's monetary critique, its documentary provenance argument, its visual-resemblance hypothesis, and its proposed jurisprudential consequences are four different layers. Its conclusion depends on bringing them together, but the evidentiary strength of one layer does not automatically establish the next.
